edition.title: Slow Burn - Friday 30 October 2026
edition.fact: Edition 25. Alphabet fell 13.2% on Thursday - its first combined revenue-and-earnings miss in nearly four years, with negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion and 2027 capex guided 'significantly' higher on a path past $300 billion (CNBC); the Sensex rose 905 points to 74,151 anyway, led by realty and FMCG, as foreign investors sold Rs 944 crore and domestic institutions bought Rs 1,924 crore; Jio Platforms' second day ran to Rs 1,490 and closed up just 0.40% at Rs 1,423.05, still above all three new broker targets; US third-quarter growth came in at 3.4% with price pressures cooling; and Equitas Small Finance Bank's chief executive resigned over a 'perception of conflict of interest,' taking 12% off the stock.
edition.intro: The 5-minute lead route is first; sections carry the detail. Yesterday this paper set two tests for Thursday: Jio holds Rs 1,400, and the Nifty reclaims 22,800. Both passed, a day early - the scoreboard is in the editor's read. The long read is Pixxel, the Bengaluru company that reads the Earth in a hundred colours - which opened a US federal subsidiary yesterday.

blocks.html: Today's long read: Reading Earth in a hundred colours - how two twenty-year-olds from BITS Pilani built India's largest space-tech company, survived a public launch scrub, and now sells to NASA. Read it here.

Alphabet's bill: -13.2% in one session: first top-and-bottom-line miss in ~4 years; free cash flow negative $9.07 billion; 2027 capex guided past $300 billion. The AI-spend reckoning arrived - selectively.
India rallied regardless: Sensex +905 to 74,151, Nifty +238 to 22,937; realty and FMCG led; FIIs sold Rs 944 crore, DIIs bought Rs 1,924 crore.
Jio day two: ran to Rs 1,490, closed Rs 1,423.05 (+0.40%), the day's most-traded stock at Rs 1,211 crore. All three new broker targets sit below the price.
A CEO quits over 'perception': Equitas SFB's P N Vasudevan resigned; the stock fell 12.4%.
America grew 3.4%: Q3 GDP beat, price gauges cooled, Amazon's AWS accelerated to +39% after the bell. Midterms on Tuesday.
Results flood: Coal India profit +53% with a Rs 10.25 dividend; Adani Ports raised guidance; Ambuja's profit fell 90% on a tax base effect.
The long read: Pixxel - from a BITS Pilani dorm to NASA contracts. Named people, dated scenes, what would prove it wrong.

1. Alphabet sinks 13.2%: the AI bill lands on the balance sheet. Alphabet reported Wednesday night its first combined revenue and earnings miss in nearly four years, and the stock fell 13.2% on Thursday, dragging the Nasdaq down 1.66% (CNBC, read in full; Reuters, read in full). The numbers: revenue $127.58 billion versus $128.22 billion expected (up 25% year on year); adjusted EPS $2.67 versus $3.02 expected; net income $26.17 billion, down from $34.98 billion a year ago - a quarter that swung to an $8.66 billion loss on its equity stakes after a $99.03 billion gain the quarter before. The figure that did the damage: free cash flow of negative $9.07 billion, against the negative $2.70 billion analysts expected, as capital expenditure ran at $51.36 billion in the quarter. Finance chief Anat Ashkenazi held 2026 capex at $195-205 billion and told analysts to expect it "to increase significantly in 2027" - a path CNBC notes runs past $300 billion next year. Long-term debt has climbed to $125.1 billion from $21.6 billion a year ago. The one beat: Google Cloud revenue more than doubled, up 103% to $30.7 billion, and the company said the Gemini app has passed one billion users (a company claim). Why it matters to you: this is the first time the market has punished, at scale, the borrow-and-burn model of AI expansion rather than rewarding the ambition - and it lands while every Indian IT services company sells into the same capex cycle. Editor's takeaway: the crash was selective - Meta rose and Amazon's cloud accelerated hours later - so the verdict is not "AI is over"; it is "show us who pays."

2. The Sensex rises 905 points on domestic money. Indian equities ignored the global wobble: the Sensex gained 905.01 points (1.24%) to 74,151.04 and the Nifty 237.90 (1.05%) to 22,936.75, closing at the day's high (Business Standard's close report). Realty led sectors, up 2.7%, with FMCG up 2.3%; autos dipped 0.24%. The Bank Nifty rose 642 points to 54,910; midcaps added 0.98% and smallcaps 0.93% (CNBC TV18). The flow story is the day's tell: foreign investors sold Rs 943.60 crore while domestic institutions bought Rs 1,924.41 crore (provisional exchange data) - one day after foreigners bought Rs 871.83 crore. Adani Ports was the Sensex's top gainer, up 5.17% on the BSE, after raising its full-year revenue and EBITDA guidance (Corporate actions, below). The easing background helped: Brent settled at $114.88, down 0.38%, on US-Iran diplomacy hopes. Why it matters to you: a rally foreigners are selling into is a rally carried by your own institutions - stronger hands in a correction, but quicker to thin out at the top. Editor's takeaway: the handoff from foreign to domestic money is the rally's engine and its fragility in the same fact.

3. Jio's second day: Rs 1,490 in the morning, +0.4% by the close. Jio Platforms ran to an intraday high of Rs 1,490 on the BSE - crossing Rs 13.5 lakh crore in market value during the session (CNBC TV18) - before fading to close at Rs 1,423.05, up just 0.40%, on Rs 1,211 crore of traded value, the most-traded stock on the board (BSE official data). The close is 27.2% above the Rs 1,119 issue price. Three brokerages initiated coverage on listing day, and all three targets sit below Thursday's close: Nomura at Rs 1,340, Motilal Oswal at Rs 1,350 and Elara Capital at Rs 1,367 (ET Markets, read in full). Their cases rest on the same lever: an industry tariff hike of 12-15% expected between November and March (Elara: the second half of FY27; Nomura: November-December), which Elara reckons lifts ARPU - average revenue per user - from Rs 214 in FY26 to Rs 257 by FY29. Nomura's supporting facts: 41.7% of India's wireless subscribers (TRAI, August), data usage 27% higher than Airtel's per user, the industry's lowest churn at 1.6%, and capex already falling toward 23% of revenue from 35%. Why it matters to you: when the optimists' targets are below the price, the market is paying for the tariff hike before it exists - the hike is now the stock's fact to deliver. Editor's takeaway: day-one buyers held (the close stayed above Rs 1,400), so the flipper thesis failed its first test - but the fade from Rs 1,490 says new money is waiting for a reason, not a story.

4. A bank CEO resigns over a perception - and the stock loses 12%. Equitas Small Finance Bank's managing director and CEO, P N Vasudevan, resigned on Thursday, writing in his letter that he was stepping down to remove an "overhang" on the stock created by a "perception of conflict of interest": his daughter is a co-promoter of Unico Housing Finance, an RBI-licensed NBFC (Hindu BusinessLine, letter read in full). He maintained there is no actual conflict - the bank has had no dealings with that NBFC beyond one short-term deposit, since repaid, and the relationship was disclosed to the board and the RBI, which approved his reappointment in July. "In my investor meetings over the past three years, I have been repeatedly asked about the perceived conflict... Sometimes perceptions are stronger than reality," he wrote. The stock fell 12.39% to Rs 56.99 on the BSE, having traded down as much as 20% intraday. Why it matters to you: governance discounts are not abstractions - here is a founder-CEO leaving over a disclosed, regulator-cleared relationship, because investors would not stop asking about it. Editor's takeaway: the resignation is the rare governance story where the 'perception' problem was cured by the exit itself - watch who the board picks, and whether the discount closes.

5. America grew 3.4% while its inflation gauges cooled - and Amazon beat after the bell. US third-quarter GDP rose at a 3.4% annual rate in the advance estimate, up from 2.2% in the second quarter, with final sales to private domestic purchasers up 4.9% (the BEA release, read in full). The same release carried the surprise: the PCE price index - the Fed's preferred gauge - rose just 2.1%, down from 5.0% in the second quarter, with core PCE at 2.5% versus 3.3%. After the closing bell, Amazon reported net sales up 12% to $201.9 billion, operating income of $28.1 billion (a record 13.9% margin), and AWS growth accelerating to 39.3% - its fastest in nearly five years - on revenue of $46.0 billion, above estimates (Amazon's own release; CNBC); AWS operating income rose 55% to $17.77 billion, and the company said it plans to buy more Nvidia chips. All of it lands five days before the midterm elections on Tuesday. Why it matters to you: strong growth plus cooling prices is the one combination that lets the Fed's hawks and doves both claim the data - December's meeting stays live, and US yields set the price of every rupee of foreign money into India. Editor's takeaway: Amazon answered the question Alphabet raised - cloud demand is real and accelerating; the market's quarrel is with who funds the build-out, not whether it is needed.

Thursday, the full picture. Sensex 74,151.04 (+1.24%), Nifty 22,936.75 (+1.05%), both closing at the day's high after opening lower; the Nifty Bank rose 642 points to 54,910 and the midcap index 567 points to 57,842 (Business Standard; CNBC TV18). In New York overnight, the Dow fell 0.59% to 52,163.07, the S&P 500 0.63% to 7,695.25 and the Nasdaq 1.66% to 26,108.35 - but the small-cap Russell 2000 rose 0.8% and advancing stocks outnumbered decliners on both exchanges, the signature of rotation rather than panic (Reuters). Gold eased 0.5% to $4,039 an ounce on the Fed hold; Brent settled at $114.88 and WTI at $102.00, both down on US-Iran diplomacy hopes. Earnings breadth remains the global counterweight: of the 253 S&P 500 companies reported so far, 81% have beaten estimates, for blended earnings growth of 31% (LSEG data carried by Reuters).

blocks.html: What Friday watches. Three clocks: the Friday results slate - 36 companies including Bank of Baroda, Bharat Electronics and Aditya Birla Capital; Jio's third session, with Rs 1,380 (Thursday's low) as the line day-one buyers defend; and the market's digestion of Amazon's beat against Alphabet's miss, which sets the tone for India's IT pack next week. Framed as what to watch, never what to buy.

EAAA India Alternatives: allotted, listing Monday. The Edelweiss group's alternatives-platform offer-for-sale (price band Rs 1,585-1,665, entirely an offer for sale by promoter Edelweiss Securities and Investments) was subscribed about 5.25 times over its three days and finalised allotment on Thursday; listing is expected on Monday 2 November (ET Now). The week's smaller mainboard issues - BLS Polymers (band Rs 142-150) and SFC Environmental (Rs 313-330) - closed on schedule on Thursday, per ET Now's tracker. As always here: grey-market premiums are unofficial and undated here on purpose, and an allotment is an outcome, not an endorsement - the five-day hold after listing is the honest test.

Jio, day two, reconciled. The fade from Rs 1,490 to Rs 1,423.05 kept every relevant record intact: +27.2% over issue, second-largest listed company, most-traded line on the board. The new fact for the file is the initiation trio - Nomura Rs 1,340, Motilal Rs 1,350, Elara Rs 1,367 - all below the market. Watch item, not a call: the tariff-hike decision those targets lean on is expected between November and March.
All figures from the official BSE end-of-day file (bhavcopy), A-group, liquidity filter applied. Reasons traced to company releases or named reports; where no driver was confirmed, the line says so.

blocks.html: Gainers, with the why. Birlasoft (+11.89% to Rs 342.65): its biggest single-day gain in more than five years (CNBC TV18), on Q2 revenue of Rs 1,416.2 crore, up 6.6% year on year and 2.7% quarter on quarter, an EBITDA margin of 15.2% held through a compensation increase, first-half order booking up 15%, and collection days at a two-year best of 51 (company release, read in full). Zensar Technologies (+8.15% to Rs 537.55): revenue of $166.2 million, up 4.1% sequentially in constant currency, EBITDA margin up 120 basis points to 15.8%, banking and financial services revenue up 17.1% year on year (company release, read in full). V-Guard Industries (+7.62% to Rs 285.15): strong Q2 results (CNBC TV18). Adani Ports (+5.17% to Rs 1,850.00): quarterly revenue up 24% and guidance raised - detail in Corporate actions.

Losers, with the why. Equitas Small Finance Bank (-12.39% to Rs 56.99): the CEO's resignation - front page, item 4. eClerx Services (-11.10% to Rs 1,660.30): a post-results selloff despite operating revenue rising 18.3% to Rs 1,188.7 crore (Business Standard) - the street had priced in more. Dalmia Bharat (-4.41% to Rs 1,407.80 on heavy Rs 186 crore value): cement's cost quarter - revenue up 4% to Rs 3,563 crore but EBITDA of Rs 493 crore hit by cost headwinds, the company said in its filing, with Ambuja's profit down 90% the same day. Hexaware Technologies fell about 6% after narrowing its EBITDA margin guidance, and RR Kabel fell 3.57% to Rs 2,127.15 after cutting its volume growth guidance (CNBC TV18). Hero MotoCorp fell 3.64% to Rs 5,107 on earnings-call commentary.

The beats. Coal India: profit up 53% year on year to Rs 6,516 crore on revenue up 20.9% to Rs 44,179 crore, EBITDA margin at 19.2% from 18% - and a second interim dividend of Rs 10.25 a share, record date Wednesday 4 November, payment by 27 November (moneycontrol's results blog, read in full). Adani Ports: revenue up 24% to Rs 11,340 crore, EBITDA up 23% to Rs 6,807 crore, profit up 18% to Rs 3,682 crore - and full-year guidance RAISED by Rs 1,000 crore each, to revenue of Rs 44,000-46,000 crore and EBITDA of Rs 26,000-27,000 crore, with capex guidance up Rs 3,000 crore to Rs 15,000-17,000 crore (company release, read in full). Kotak Mahindra Bank (Saturday): standalone profit up 29.5% to Rs 4,212 crore on net interest income of Rs 8,459 crore; margin at 4.31%, down from 4.54% a year ago; gross NPAs improved to 1.04% (CNBC TV18). Also strong: Acme Solar (profit +133% to Rs 268 crore), Milky Mist (+174% to Rs 78 crore), Laurus Labs (above estimates, up 3%), Blue Star (profit +25.5%).

The misses - and the honest middle. Ambuja Cements: profit down 90% to Rs 236 crore - but the year-ago quarter held a Rs 1,697 crore tax-provision reversal, so the like-for-like decline is far smaller; fuel and logistics costs did the real damage (moneycontrol, read in full). Suzlon Energy: profit down 69% to Rs 394 crore even as revenue rose 26% - margin fell 400 basis points to 14.7%. IEX: profit up 12.9% to Rs 139 crore on revenue up 8.5%. Vedanta's oil-and-gas arm: profit down 21% quarter on quarter to Rs 746 crore. eClerx (revenue +18.3%, stock -11%) sits in Movers above. The pattern of the season so far: profit pools are moving toward companies that own their input costs - Coal India's royalties, Adani Ports' 72.5% domestic-port margins - and away from fuel-price takers.

Dates for the diary. Coal India's Rs 10.25 interim has its record date on Wednesday 4 November (payment by 27 November). Infosys's Rs 26 interim record date is Tuesday 3 November, payment 11 November. HUL's Rs 19 interim: record 12 November, payment 25 November. Tech Mahindra's 1:1 bonus record date remains unannounced as of this morning. Friday's board-meeting slate holds 36 results, including Bank of Baroda, Bharat Electronics and Aditya Birla Capital (quarterlyresults.in).

1. The Rs 2,868-crore handoff: who actually bought Thursday. Foreign investors sold Rs 943.60 crore of Indian equities on a 905-point up day; domestic institutions bought Rs 1,924.41 crore (CNBC TV18, provisional exchange data). The mechanism worth holding: index levels are set at the margin, so the identity of the marginal buyer decides what the rally is made of. Domestic buying is largely systematic - monthly SIP money that arrives regardless of headlines - while foreign selling is discretionary and fast. A market carried by systematic money grinds; a market carried by discretionary money swings. One day proves nothing, and the provisional figures get revised, but Wednesday's foreigners-bought / Thursday's foreigners-sold pair says the marginal foreign rupee is trading this market, not investing in it. Editor's takeaway: celebrate the close, respect the composition - the bid underneath you is mechanical, and mechanical bids pause the day salaries or sentiment stutter.

2. The Fed's data fight, now with both weapons loaded. Thursday's GDP release armed both sides of December: growth at 3.4% with final domestic demand up 4.9% is the hawks' case (two officials dissented for a quarter-point hike on Wednesday, per the Fed's own statement); PCE inflation cooling to 2.1% from 5.0% is the doves' (BEA, read in full). The mechanism: the statement itself says "the accumulation of more information" will determine the stance - which makes every print between now and the December meeting a live vote. For India the transmission is unchanged: US yields near 5% are the gravity on foreign flows (item 1) and on the RBI's room to ease. What would make this read wrong: a November inflation print that re-accelerates - the hawks' dissent becomes the base case in one morning. Editor's takeaway: the Fed held rates but handed the calendar to the data - Thursday gave both sides a number to quote.

3. Crude's premium leaks again - five days before the vote. Brent settled at $114.88 (-0.38%) and WTI at $102.00 (-0.76%) on Thursday, both down more than $2 intraday at one point, as US-Iran diplomacy hopes offset supply-disruption fears (Reuters). This is the third round trip in two weeks: strike fears fill the premium, diplomacy leaks it. The standing conversion - about $2 billion a year on India's import bill per dollar of crude - makes each $3 swing a $6-billion annualized question for the current account. The reported calendar (the Wall Street Journal story this paper carried Wednesday: Washington told Gulf states to prepare for action after the 3 November midterms) remains on the board as a report, not a fact; while it stands, the premium's floor is roughly $112-113, by this paper's read. What removes the premium at the root: a signed deal. Editor's takeaway: the oil market is pricing an election, not a war - treat Tuesday's result as the crude position nobody is hedging.

Pixxel opens a US federal subsidiary. Bengaluru's Pixxel announced Pixxel Federal on Thursday: a US subsidiary to sell its Earth-observation satellites, software and geospatial intelligence to American civilian, defence and intelligence agencies, led by Allyson Jenkins, its former public-sector vice president (company release, read in full). The context that makes it more than an office opening: Pixxel closed a $100-million Series C in September - co-led by Temasek and Seraphim, the largest space-tech round ever raised in India - and already counts NASA and the US National Reconnaissance Office among its contract partners. Today's long read is the whole Pixxel story. Insight: sovereign space sales are won inside the buyer's own flag - a US subsidiary with US-cleared leadership is not expansion theatre, it is the procurement requirement.

Vegafin's Rs 1,000-crore MSME lending bet. Premji Invest, Norwest Venture Partners and Lok Capital have committed up to Rs 1,000 crore to Vegafin, an AI-first MSME-lending platform founded by ICICI Bank veteran Bijith Bhaskar - starting with a majority stake in Bizloan, a Gurugram NBFC that lends secured loans to small businesses (Premji Invest's release, read in full). The mechanism: buy the licence and the loan book, rebuild underwriting on digital workflows and data-led credit decisions, and use the NBFC's on-ground network for distribution. It is the largest Indian startup cheque of October - in a week that otherwise saw about $188 million across 14 announced rounds. Insight: the platform-plus-NBFC structure is becoming the default fintech playbook - the licence is the moat, the software is the margin.

Startup idea (one, as specified). Hyperspectral crop-insurance loss assessment. India's crop insurance settles claims on yield estimates and manual crop-cutting experiments - slow, disputed, and expensive to administer. A constellation like Pixxel's Fireflies reads fields in hundreds of light bands: crop type, stress and waterlogging are measurable from orbit, plot by plot, within days of an event. The product: a per-plot damage index sold to insurers and state agriculture departments as the settlement input. Who pays: insurers first (cheaper, faster claims), then the scheme itself if the index survives audit. First step: one district pilot for one insured crop, scored against the season's actual crop-cutting data to prove the index tracks ground truth. What would make it wrong: revisit frequency - if the satellites pass too rarely to catch the damage window, the index misses exactly the events it exists to price.

Opportunity watch. Nothing verified this cycle clears the bar for a specific grant, programme or competition deadline worth your time this week; the honest entry is an empty slot rather than a padded one.

1. The sorting day: funded AI versus borrowed AI. Thursday's tape split the AI trade in two. On one side: Alphabet -13.2% (negative free cash flow, debt up five-fold, 2027 capex guided past $300 billion), chip stocks down 2.0%, ServiceNow down 27% and Fortinet down 20% on their own quarters. On the other: Meta up 2.0%, Amazon's AWS accelerating to 39.3% growth with record margins hours after the close, the Russell 2000 up 0.8%, and more stocks rising than falling on both US exchanges (Reuters, read in full). The mechanism the market applied: AI spending funded by accelerating cloud revenue (Amazon, Microsoft) is a business; AI spending funded by borrowing against hoped-for returns is a bet. Baird's Ross Mayfield put it plainly: the market is saying the cracks are in the AI story's financing, not in every corner of the market. With 81% of reporting companies beating estimates so far (LSEG), the earnings season itself is fine - the question is who pays for the build-out. Editor's takeaway: watch the capex-to-cloud-growth ratio, not the headlines - that ratio is now the stock price.

2. Radar. OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Terra reached Amazon Bedrock on Monday (AWS model card): visual reasoning and computer use, with OpenAI's own evaluation claiming a 15-point gain over GPT-5.6 Terra on its agents benchmark and three-times-faster task completion than GPT-6 Astra - vendor numbers, dated and labelled as such. Particle AI's Particle-1 landed on Vercel's AI Gateway on Wednesday (Vercel changelog): a coding model post-trained on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, tuned to finish engineering tasks in fewer tokens, with a one-million-token context window. Google said Wednesday its Gemini app has passed one billion users - the company's own figure. Amazon told analysts it plans to buy more Nvidia chips (CNBC). X was not accessible for cross-checking; the radar is built from official blogs and says so.

This week shipped three models you might build on - Terra on Monday, Particle-1 on Wednesday, Carbon the Wednesday before - and the only durable engineering response to that cadence is a harness, not a favourite. Put a gateway or a thin adapter between your code and the model API, so swapping providers is a configuration line, not a rewrite; pin the model version in every production call, because "latest" is a moving target that will silently change your outputs; and keep a small test set of your own tasks - twenty prompts with known-good answers - that you run against every new model before adopting it. The economics reinforce the same discipline: when OpenAI sells computer-use tokens at half its predecessor's price and Particle-1's pitch is finishing in fewer tokens, the cost of a task keeps falling - which means the expensive part of your system is no longer the model, it is the failure you did not catch. Spend the savings on verification: run the agent twice on anything load-bearing and diff the outputs. The vendors will keep shipping; the harness is the part you still own.

Automate one number you check by hand. Friday is automation day, and this paper's own method is the specimen. Pick one closing price you look up daily - a holding, an index, USD-INR - and stop looking it up. Steps: (1) after 6 PM, download the day's BSE bhavcopy CSV (bseindia.com, BhavCopy section - the exchange's official end-of-day file); (2) open it in any spreadsheet or a five-line script and filter to your stock's row; (3) write the four numbers you care about - open, high, low, close - into one dated line of a running log; (4) set a reminder for tomorrow's 6 PM until the habit holds. Time: twenty minutes the first day, two minutes after. What a good result looks like: a two-week log you built yourself, so that when any app, tip or headline quotes you a price, you have your own official number to check it against. The automation is trivial; the habit of going to the primary source is the skill - it is the same discipline this paper applies to every figure it prints.

In 1985, Hersh Shefrin and Meir Statman gave a name to the most common mistake in retail investing: the disposition effect - the tendency to sell winners too early and hold losers too long. The human story is in the proof. In the late 1990s a Berkeley researcher named Terrance Odean obtained something no one had studied before: the complete trading records of about 10,000 households at a US discount brokerage. When he counted, in his 1998 study (the paper itself), how often investors realised their winners versus their losers, the winners were sold at roughly one-and-a-half times the rate of the losers - not because the losers recovered, but because selling a loss means admitting one. The mechanism is psychological, not analytical: a gain feels like a prize to lock in, a loss feels like a mistake to postpone, so portfolios drift toward their worst positions while their best ones are cashed out. Hold it up to this week's tape: Jio's day-two sellers at Rs 1,490 were locking a prize two days after allotment - the disposition effect predicts exactly that behaviour after a 27% pop, and it predicts the counterparty too: the buyer at Rs 1,490 is often someone who just sold a different winner. Sixty-second recall, closed book: (1) Who named the disposition effect, and when? (2) What did Odean's brokerage data show? (3) Why do investors hold losers? Answers: Shefrin and Statman, 1985; winners were sold about 1.5 times as often as losers across some 10,000 households; because realising a loss means admitting the mistake - the pain is psychological, not financial.

groups.heading: Term of the day: free float

blocks.html: The shares of a company actually available to trade - total shares minus those locked up with promoters, governments and long-term strategic holders. Price is set where available shares meet demand, so a small float makes big moves cheap: when demand arrives for a stock with almost nothing for sale, the price has to travel far to find a seller. Jio Platforms is the live example - its free float is under 3% (Motilal Oswal's initiation note), part of why a Rs 13-lakh-crore company can swing Rs 110 intraday on its second day. Read floats before you read volumes: a high traded value on a tiny float is churn, not conviction.

Week one closes with the board's first fill ahead. Every live name on one board: terms in rows, nothing buried in prose. Conditional setups only - entry is a zone, never a market order. No orders are placed, ever; every call is scored by the standing rules in the ledger File. Every published setup stays until its target or its stop resolves it, with status kept honest daily.

blocks.html: Setup slots 2 to 5 are empty today. Nothing else cleared the verification bar; an empty slot is a result, not a gap. Thursday's read, with per-share prices: HCLTech (Rs 1,411.50) held its gain - the fill at Rs 1,378.00 (effective Rs 1,382.13 after the 0.3% cost illustration) is ahead 2.12% net, with the day's high of Rs 1,421.95 still short of the Rs 1,466.80 target and the low of Rs 1,390.50 far above the Rs 1,346.90 stop. Kotak (Rs 457.00) ran the six-factor screen as the candidate: momentum - strong, its best session since the results, closing near the day's high; volume - 17.5 lakh shares against 2.1 lakh the day before, an eight-fold expansion; trend - firmly above the Rs 437.55 trigger; catalyst - Saturday's Q2, standalone profit up 29.5%; fundamentals - the honest thin spot, with net interest margin falling to 4.31% from 4.53% a quarter ago; industry - banks led Thursday's tape. It stays a candidate, not a setup: at Rs 457 the entry has not structured into a zone with a defensible stop, and chasing a 3.9% up-day is exactly what this paper's concept section warns about. Infosys (Rs 1,143.45) rose 1.81%, holding comfortably above its Rs 1,109.70 tripwire - the absorption thesis intact. ONGC (Rs 225.40) is mid-coil; JSW Steel (Rs 1,251.20) holds well above its floor. Tech Mahindra stays shelved above your Rs 1,500 cap.

blocks.html: Scoreboard first. Yesterday's read deferred the liquidity verdict to day two, on two conditions: Jio holds Rs 1,400 and the Nifty reclaims 22,800. Thursday met both, a day early - Jio closed Rs 1,423.05, the Nifty 22,936.75 - so the deferred verdict now reads positive: the debut is adding liquidity despite the global tape, and the primary-market window stays open into November. The new variable is the financing question Alphabet just made expensive: if the market is repricing borrowed AI ambition, every richly valued growth story - India's new listings included - gets a higher bar to clear. The falsifiable read for the coming week: if Jio holds Rs 1,380 (Thursday's low) through the US midterm vote on Tuesday and Brent stays under $117, the window holds into Diwali and the results season finishes the year on the front foot. If Jio closes under Rs 1,300, the day-one buyers were exit liquidity after all, and the defensiveness of late October returns. Confidence: moderate. What would change my mind by Monday: an Alphabet-style repricing crossing into India through the IT pack - that is the channel to watch, not the index.

1. The midterms, Tuesday. America votes on 3 November: 35 Senate seats are up, and Democrats need a net gain of four to take the chamber; the House fight runs mostly on Republican-held turf (NBC News). The market angle is the calendar: the Fed held this week and was reported to be waiting out the vote before any move, and this week's Wall Street Journal story put any US action on Iran after the same date. Watch for: crude's reaction on Wednesday morning IST. What would change the story: a decisive either-way result priced calmly - the risk is a contested count, not a party.

2. December's Fed, armed both ways. Thursday handed the hawks 3.4% growth and the doves 2.1% PCE inflation; two officials dissented for a hike on Wednesday (the Fed's statement). Watch for: the November inflation and jobs prints - each one is now a live vote on December. What would change the story: one re-accelerating price print, which converts the dissent into the base case.

3. Anthropic's roadshow range. The reported trading window - week of 16 November - approaches; the amended filing with a price range is the next document. Watch for: the range versus the last private mark, and versus what Jio's debut proved a first day can do. What would change the story: a range below the private mark - a public down-round for the AI leader, landing in the same fortnight the market punished Alphabet's AI spending.

Two wire conflicts resolved in favour of the primary source: AP's overnight report carried the S&P 500 as down 0.3% while Reuters' close report showed -48.73 points to 7,695.25, which is 0.63% - the internally consistent Reuters figure is used. A Reuters line characterised Thursday's data as price growth gaining heat; the BEA release itself shows the PCE price index cooling to 2.1% from 5.0%, so the BEA figures are used and the characterisation dropped.

Jio Platforms' prices are BSE official prints throughout (close Rs 1,423.05, high Rs 1,490.00, low Rs 1,380.50); NSE prints differ by paise and intraday timing. Sector moves are Nifty sectoral indices as carried in Business Standard and CNBC TV18 close reports - NSE surfaces were not accessed.
Kotak Mahindra Bank's Q2 figures are as carried by CNBC TV18 and the Economic Times; the bank's own BSE filing exists but was not read in full this cycle.
Alphabet's one-billion Gemini users, OpenAI's benchmark gains and Particle AI's token-efficiency claims are vendor claims and are labelled and dated as such. X was not accessible for cross-checking.
Indian prices are from BSE's official end-of-day file only. Index levels are as carried in the named wraps. The FII/DII figures are provisional exchange data and may be revised.

Markets coverage is research, not advice: the setup board's levels are conditional research triggers with published invalidation and targets, not recommendations to buy or sell. No orders are placed; the ledger books results only on actual fills.
